questions.prompt: Complete: "If you ___ the 8 o'clock bus, you will arrive on time."
questions.explanation: The blank is in the if clause, which takes the simple present: If you catch the 8 o'clock bus. "will catch" is the classic mistake — will goes only in the main clause; "caught" is the simple past; "catches" is for he, she or it, not you.

questions.prompt: Complete: "If Yasmine revises tonight, she ___ the English test tomorrow."
questions.explanation: The blank is in the main clause, which gives the result with will + base verb: she will pass the English test. "passes" and "passed" forget will; "will passes" keeps an -s after will, but after will the verb is always bare.

questions.prompt: In "We will take the metro if it rains", which clause states the condition?
questions.explanation: The condition is the clause that starts with if: "if it rains". "We will take the metro" is tempting because it comes first, but it is the main clause — the result. The place of a clause does not decide its job; the word if does.

questions.prompt: Put the if clause first: "I will help you if you ask me." Choose the sentence written as this chapter teaches (tenses and comma):

options.text: If you ask me, I will help you.
If you ask me I will help you.
If, you ask me I will help you.
If you will ask me, I help you.

questions.explanation: "If you ask me, I will help you." — the if clause now comes first, so a comma closes it, and the tenses stay the same. Without the comma the rule of this chapter is broken; a comma straight after "If" is misplaced; "If you will ask me, I help you" moves will into the if clause.

questions.prompt: Complete with the negative: "If Ali ___ (not hurry), he will miss the train."
questions.explanation: In the if clause the negative is don't / doesn't + base verb, and Ali is he: If Ali doesn't hurry. "won't hurry" puts will in the if clause; "don't" is for I, you, we, they; "doesn't hurries" adds a second -s, but doesn't already carries it.

questions.prompt: Complete: "If there are repairs on the road, you ___ back home before one o'clock."
questions.explanation: The main clause gives a negative result with won't + base verb: you won't be back home. "won't to be" adds to after won't; "won't are" conjugates the verb, which must stay bare; "don't be" is not the negative future.
